explanations.explanation: I see why you'd think so, because the kings and merchants really do weep over Babylon (Revelation 18:9-11). But John hears something very different in heaven. The voices there are shouting, “Hallelujah! Salvation and glory and power belong to our God!” Two crowds, same city, and not one tissue in the second crowd.

You caught it, friend. The kings and merchants weep and mourn over Babylon (Revelation 18:9-11), but that's a different crowd. The voices John hears in heaven are shouting, “Hallelujah! Salvation and glory and power belong to our God!” That is the sound of people who are NOT crying into their sleeves.

explanations.answer: His judgments are true and just
explanations.explanation: Right on the money, baker. The voices say, “For His judgments are true and just.” That's the reason behind all the shouting. They aren't praising because of a deal or a surprise, but because of who God is and what He has done.

explanations.answer: The kings have made peace with Him
explanations.explanation: Not what the voices say, friend. The kings of the earth show up earlier in Revelation weeping over Babylon (Revelation 18:9), and nothing here says they made peace with anybody. The reason in heaven is this: “For His judgments are true and just.” I once spent a week sure my oven was broken when the pilot light was just off, so I know how easy it is to grab the wrong cause.

explanations.answer: The merchants have turned back to Him
explanations.explanation: That one isn't in the text, baker. The merchants of the earth are the ones weeping and mourning over Babylon (Revelation 18:11). The voices in heaven give a different reason: “For His judgments are true and just.” Their praise is about God's judgments, not about anyone coming back.

That's the word, friend. The voices say, “He has avenged the blood of His servants that was poured out by her hand.” I think this part of the passage is a heavy one, and it's worth a quiet moment. God sees what was done to His servants, and the voices in heaven say He has answered it.

That's the opposite of what the voices say. They declare, “He has avenged the blood of His servants that was poured out by her hand.” Nothing in these verses says anything was overlooked. This is a heavy part, so I'll just say it plainly: the word is avenged.

Close to the right neighborhood, but not the word. The voices say, “He has avenged the blood of His servants that was poured out by her hand.” Forgotten isn't anywhere in that line. The word the text gives is avenged, and it's a heavy one.

Not yet, baker, because the voices have more to say. Verse 3 says a second time they call out, “Hallelujah! Her smoke rises forever and ever.” So the first shout wasn't the whole thing. Heaven is just getting warmed up, like a oven on its second preheat.

Correct, friend. The text says a second time they call out, “Hallelujah! Her smoke rises forever and ever.” One shout wasn't enough for them. I respect that, because I've never stopped at one batch either.

Yes, baker. The twenty-four elders and the four living creatures fell down and worshiped God who sits on the throne. They're at the throne, so they go straight to the ground. When I want to feel humble, I hop around my bakery, but this is the real thing.

explanations.answer: Stand at a distance and weep
explanations.explanation: That's the mourning over Babylon, friend, not the throne room. Standing at a distance belongs to the people grieving the city's fall (Revelation 18:10). The elders and the living creatures do something else in this passage. They fall down and worship God who sits on the throne, saying, “Amen, Hallelujah!”

Dust on the head shows up in the mourning over Babylon (Revelation 18:19), so it belongs to that scene. The elders and the living creatures aren't mourning here. Verse 4 says they fell down and worshiped God who sits on the throne. Wrong scene, same room for cleanup though, I'd bet.

explanations.answer: All who serve and fear Him
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. The voice from the throne says, “Praise our God, all you who serve Him, and those who fear Him, small and great alike!” Notice how wide that circle is. Nobody gets left standing outside it.

The elders already worshiped in verse 4, and then this voice speaks to a much bigger group. It says, “Praise our God, all you who serve Him, and those who fear Him, small and great alike!” So it's not a small invite list. I've never seen a guest list that big, and I've baked for a lot of Tuesdays.

The text doesn't narrow it down like that, baker. The voice from the throne says, “Praise our God, all you who serve Him, and those who fear Him, small and great alike!” That reaches everyone who serves Him and fears Him. It doesn't name one group only.

You got it, baker. The voice calls on those who fear Him, “small and great alike!” Small and great, together in the same praise. If a stamper in the back of a drawer can be invited, believe me, small counts.
Strong is a good word, but it isn't the one here. The voice from the throne says, “small and great alike!” So the call goes to the small and the great together. Nobody has to flex to get in.

Wise sounds right, friend, but the text says something else. The voice says, “small and great alike!” It isn't sorting people by how clever they are. Good thing too, because I once tried to bake with the oven off.

explanations.answer: The Lord our God the Almighty reigns
explanations.explanation: Exactly right, baker. The voices cry out, “For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns.” That's their reason for the Hallelujah. And a roar like many waters and thunder? I think that's a pretty good place to say it.

explanations.answer: The Lord our God has gathered the nations
explanations.explanation: That isn't what these voices say, friend. Their reason is, “For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns.” Gathering the nations isn't mentioned in these verses. The reason is simply that He reigns.

explanations.answer: The Lord our God has opened the heavens
explanations.explanation: Not in this verse, baker. The voices give their reason plainly: “For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns.” Nothing about opening the heavens is part of that cry. Their Hallelujah is about His reign.
That's it, baker. They say, “For the marriage of the Lamb has come.” That's the big news behind the rejoicing. And it's why my ovens never go cold.

Not here, friend. Right after “Let us rejoice and be glad,” the voices say what has come: “For the marriage of the Lamb has come.” No harvest in this verse. The cause of the joy is the marriage of the Lamb.

That's not part of what they say, baker. After the call to rejoice, the voices say, “For the marriage of the Lamb has come.” Nobody mentions a temple being rebuilt here. The marriage of the Lamb is the reason.

Yes, friend. The voices say, “His bride has made herself ready.” That's the same thing Revelation says about the bride, and it's why I help bakers get ready, not do it for them. Nobody can take a bath for you either.
Known is a fair guess, but it isn't the word. The verse says, “His bride has made herself ready.” It's about being prepared for the wedding. I've been known for plenty, mostly crumbs.

Humble is a lovely word, baker, but the text says something else. The voices declare, “His bride has made herself ready.” Ready is the word for the wedding. I wear a tall chef's hat and I'm still working on humble.

explanations.answer: The righteous acts of the saints
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. The text says, “For the fine linen she wears is the righteous acts of the saints.” So the bright, pure clothing stands for what the saints have done. It's good to see a verse that explains its own picture.

explanations.answer: The riches of the great city
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that, friend. It gives its own answer: “For the fine linen she wears is the righteous acts of the saints.” The linen stands for righteous acts, not for riches. A shopping trip would have been easier.

explanations.answer: The prayers of the twenty-four elders
explanations.explanation: It's a good guess, since the elders just worshiped, but the verse says otherwise. It reads, “For the fine linen she wears is the righteous acts of the saints.” The linen is the righteous acts. The elders aren't mentioned in that verse.

explanations.answer: Those invited to the marriage supper
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The angel tells John to write, “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.” The blessing goes to the invited. I know that feeling well, and I'd tell you all about it, but I'm trying to keep this short.

explanations.answer: Those seated closest to the throne
explanations.explanation: Seating isn't mentioned, friend. The angel says, “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.” The blessing is about being invited. Nobody's working a seating chart here.

explanations.answer: Those who kept watch through the night
explanations.explanation: That isn't what the angel says, baker. John is told to write, “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.” The blessing goes to those invited. No night shift required.

Yes, baker. After telling John to write, the angel says, “These are the true words of God.” That puts a seal on the blessing about the supper. When the words are true, I don't need to add anything fancy.

Actually, friend, the angel does say it. After telling John to write, he says, “These are the true words of God.” So the blessing about the marriage supper comes with that assurance. It's worth reading twice.
The angel does the opposite, friend. When John falls at his feet to worship, the angel says, “Do not do that!” He doesn't accept it. He stops John right there.
You've got it, baker. John falls at the angel's feet, and the angel says, “Do not do that!” He stops it on the spot. If I tried that, I'd be stopped by my own mustache.
That's right, baker. The angel says, “I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers who rely on the testimony of Jesus.” He puts himself right next to John. It's hard to get humbler than that.

No title like that, friend. The angel actually says, “I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers who rely on the testimony of Jesus.” He's bringing himself down to John's level, not up. A king would have said yes to the worship.

That isn't how he describes himself. The angel says, “I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers who rely on the testimony of Jesus.” That's the whole title he gives. I think it says a lot about him.
Yes, baker. The angel says, “Worship God!” John's pointed to the right One. Every time I hear that line, I put my mustache down and listen.

That's what the angel just refused, friend. He told John, “Do not do that!” and then said, “Worship God!” So the answer points past the angel, to God. An angel pointing away from himself is a good sign.
The elders are in the passage, but they aren't who the angel points to. He says, “Worship God!” The elders themselves fell down and worshiped God in verse 4. Even they point the same way.
